title: When Math Stops Being the Measure of Intelligence
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Trammell asks what happens to our idea of intelligence when mathematical ability, long the clearest proxy for brilliance, becomes abundant through AI. He cites a Gemini model reaching gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad and Jensen Huang's remark that forgotten basic math may not matter. His argument is that intelligence is partly a function of scarcity, and that calculators, spreadsheets and search engines have already devalued skills once considered rare. He turns to CEOs as a preview, since a good chief executive has never been the best analyst in the room but the person who synthesizes, balances interests and decides. If analytical horsepower becomes cheap, he says, leaders should look for and develop the ability to frame problems, exercise judgment, understand people and turn knowledge into action. The same shift, he suggests, will eventually change how we think about education and national competitiveness.
points: Trammell argues that the prestige of mathematical ability rests partly on its scarcity, so abundant machine math weakens it as a proxy for who is smartest.
The CEO role already models the shift, because executive intelligence depends on knowing what to do with answers other people produce.
The hardest leadership questions, such as firing a long-serving executive or abandoning a costly product, are rarely mathematical and AI does not settle them.
Leaders should reorient talent development toward problem framing, judgment, cross-domain connection and understanding people.
The guiding question moves from who can do the math to who can use the machines that do the math to accomplish something important.
quotes: What we regard as intelligence is partly a function of scarcity. Mathematical ability has historically carried such prestige because it is difficult and relatively rare among humans.
Technology has done this before. Calculators reduced the value of doing long calculations by hand. Spreadsheets reduced the value of constructing financial models manually.

In other words, the CEO’s intelligence has always depended less on personally producing every answer than on knowing what to do with the answers other people produce. AI pushes more of us in that direction.

But none of those activities settles the question. Someone still has to decide which considerations matter most, reconcile conflicting information, understand the people involved, and act under uncertainty.

If analytical horsepower becomes abundant, the scarce forms of intelligence inside an organization may increasingly be the ability to frame the right problem, exercise judgment, connect ideas across domains, recognize good work, understand people, and turn knowledge into action.
The scarce capability will increasingly be not producing the technically correct answer, but applying judgment to it: What question should we be asking? Which answers matter?
